sections.title: The moon condition
sections.line: The albedo as the silver or moon condition, the daybreak and the ortus solis: CW12 ¶334, CW16 ¶484.

quotes.quote: It is the silver or moon condition, which still has to be raised to the sun condition.
The albedo is, so to speak, the daybreak, but not till the rubedo is it sunrise.
The whitening (albedo or dealbatio) is likened to the ortus solis, the sunrise; it is the light, the illumination, that follows the darkness.

sections.title: Illumination and Luna
sections.line: Illumination, Luna and the anima, and the moon as prefiguration of the self: CW14 ¶220, ¶218 and ¶217.

quotes.quote: From the darkness of the unconscious comes the light of illumination, the albedo.
This role of Luna devolves upon the anima, as she personifies the plurality of archetypes
The moon with her antithetical nature is, in a sense, a prototype of individuation, a prefiguration of the self

sections.title: Washing, peacock's tail, salt
sections.line: The ablutio and the cauda pavonis leading to the whitening (CW12 ¶334); salt and ash as synonyms for the albedo (CW14 ¶320).

quotes.quote: From this the washing (ablutio, baptisma) either leads direct to the whitening (albedo), or else the soul (anima) released at the “death” is reunited with the dead body and brings about its resurrection, or again the “many colours” (omnes colores), or “peacock’s tail” (cauda pavonis), lead to the one white colour that contains all colours.
Salt as much as ash is a synonym for the albedo (or dealbatio), and is identical with “the white stone, the white sun, the full moon, the fruitful white earth, cleansed and calcined.”

sections.title: The whitest white
sections.line: The Rosarium on the whitest white (CW16 ¶514); the albedo as the climax of the work for many alchemists (CW14 ¶388).

quotes.quote: Therefore the artist must wait until he sees the Tincture covered over with its other colour, as with the whitest white
They all unite in the albedo, which for many alchemists was the climax of the work.
